correctness.rationale: The spherical width is exactly the maximum of d(d+1) type-A oriented unit roots. The root Gram count has d(d+1)(d-1) unordered pairs at angle pi/3; all other pairs are separated at least pi/2. Three-cap intersections require t<=sqrt(2/3) via norm bound, so two-term inclusion-exclusion is exact on the specified interval. Conditioning on the bisector coordinate supplies the beta lens integral; tangent-coordinate scaling yields the exact d/2 overlap exponent and stated coefficient, including d=2. The independently rerun verifier passed 66 grouped checks and 360,000 Haar samples per dimension in d=2..5; these corroborate, but do not replace, the proof.

originality.rationale: The proven finite-dimensional upper-width survival law, root-cap overlap thresholds, and exact first-overlap coefficient were not stated or implied as an immediate special case by the materially inspected primary works. The existing simplex moment formulas determine the law abstractly but do not calculate its exact finite-dimensional cap union or phase boundaries. Published cube and octahedron laws involve different support-direction configurations. Historical risk remains because some older texts and unindexed sources were not inspected.
residual_risks: Full text of the 1992 Affentranger–Schneider random-projection paper was not accessible; its abstract does not indicate the same claim.
A historical or unindexed study of tetrahedral width or oriented-root cap unions could have computed overlapping results.
Implicit all-moment characterizations of width distributions are already published; explicit new structure should not be mistaken for the first definition of the law.

value.rationale: Random directional width of a regular simplex is a natural geometric projection and Gaussian extreme-range invariant. The result gives a complete nontrivial upper distribution regime in all dimensions, two sharp overlap transitions, and an exact leading singular correction of order delta^(d/2) with combinatorial coefficient. This is a structural distribution theorem, not a single numerical example or a known moment renaming.
